title: Massapootupaug
summary: Massapootupaug is a western Southampton placename connected with a 1662 Shinnecock conveyance boundary near Niamack, Canoe Place, and the old gutt.
why_this_matters: A 1662 land deed transferring Shinnecock territory to Captain Topping used the Algonquian name Massapootupaug to mark the westernmost boundary of the south side. Examining these early colonial transactions reveals how indigenous leaders actively negotiated their borders, while also showing how Native place names were permanently inscribed into the legal foundation of Long Island's towns.
introduction_content: Massapootupaug belongs to the bay-and-inlet geography of western Southampton. A 1662 land record used the name within a much larger description extending from Niamack toward an old inlet; the name should not be read as an exact modern parcel. Tooker, pp. 113–114
history_content: Tooker reconsidered his own earlier translation. In 1911 he associated the name, tentatively, with East Bay south of Westhampton and a former opening through the barrier beach, and favored a “great bay” interpretation over his earlier meadow reading. His uncertainty matters: a changing inlet can help explain a place name without identifying a surviving boundary. Tooker, pp. 113–114
translation_content:
The recorded variant is Masspootupaug. Massapootupaug is interpreted as a great bay or cove with a narrow inlet from a river or sea, while noting that an earlier interpretation as great boggy meadow was later reconsidered.

Why Place Names Matter

“Personal names and place names are like baskets that hold a piece of history. They connect to ancient histories that often go back to the origin stories of the First Nation who holds them.”

— First Nations Education Steering Committee and First Nations Schools Association, BC First Peoples 12 Teacher Resource Guide (2022), Printed p. 152; PDF page 152, Place Names section

A 1662 land deed transferring Shinnecock territory to Captain Topping used the Algonquian name Massapootupaug to mark the westernmost boundary of the south side. Examining these early colonial transactions reveals how indigenous leaders actively negotiated their borders, while also showing how Native place names were permanently inscribed into the legal foundation of Long Island's towns.
whereintheworld_content: The shaded area is a broad orientation to the western Southampton bay landscape, not a reconstruction of the 1662 tract. Tooker’s proposed connection with East Bay and an old inlet remains an interpretation. Neither the modern shoreline nor the polygon establishes the position of that seventeenth-century opening. Tooker, pp. 113–114
